common_name: Firefly Coral Bells (Fragrant Bright Red Heuchera sanguinea Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Firefly is one of the older named selections of the flower-focused species Heuchera sanguinea, chosen for unusually fragrant blooms rather than foliage color.

directions: Firefly forms a tidy mound of rounded, scalloped, plain green leaves and sends up wiry, airy scapes carrying loose sprays of small, bell-shaped, bright true-red flowers with a light, sweet fragrance uncommon among coral bells cultivars. Bloom is heaviest in late spring and early summer, and shearing the spent flower stalks back to the foliage often coaxes a lighter second flush later in the season. Unlike the many foliage-bred modern heuchera hybrids grown mainly for colored leaves, Firefly is prized for its flower display and is a reliable draw for hummingbirds and bees. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and flowering.
sources: Chicago Botanic Garden Plant Evaluation Notes

common_name: Splendens Coral Bells (Classic Deep Red Heuchera sanguinea Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; Splendens needs the same sharp drainage as the species and resents heavy, wet clay through winter.

directions: One of the oldest named selections of Heuchera sanguinea still in commerce, Splendens carries deeper, more saturated crimson-red flowers than the species and holds them in noticeably fuller, showier clusters on tall, wiry scapes above rounded, silver-marbled green leaves. Bloom runs from late spring into early summer and draws hummingbirds reliably wherever it is planted. Because it flowers so heavily, plants benefit from a light topdressing of compost each spring to sustain vigor, and division every three to four years keeps the crown from becoming congested and reduces flower count. Excellent drainage is essential, since the species and its older cultivars are markedly less tolerant of soggy winter soil than many modern foliage heucheras.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Heuchera Species and Cultivars

common_name: White Cloud Coral Bells (Classic White-Flowered Heuchera sanguinea Cultivar)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial shade; White Cloud gives the species' classic flower display in a clean white rather than the typical red-to-coral range.

directions: White Cloud breaks from the reds and corals typical of Heuchera sanguinea, opening abundant sprays of small, pure white, bell-shaped flowers on slender scapes above rounded, scalloped, silver-veined green leaves. It blooms profusely from late spring into early summer, and the pale flower color reads especially well against darker-foliaged neighbors or in evening gardens. Like other sanguinea-type coral bells it wants sharper drainage than the heavier-textured foliage hybrids and struggles in wet winter clay. Cutting back spent scapes tidies the clump and can encourage a modest rebloom later in summer, and dividing every three to four years keeps plants floriferous.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension — Heuchera Species and Cultivars

planting.note: Plant container-grown divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade in spring or early fall; Brass Lantern's deeply cut, maple-like leaf shape sets it apart from the rounder-leaved heucherella cultivars in the same breeding lines.

directions: Brass Lantern is grown chiefly for its deeply lobed, sharply cut, maple-shaped leaves, which emerge a warm amber-copper and deepen toward burnished brass and bronze tones as the season progresses, brightening in cooler weather. The dissected leaf shape gives it a finer, lacier texture than the many rounded-leaf heucherella selections, making it a useful textural contrast planted among broader-leaved hostas and heucheras. Airy stems carry small, creamy-white flowers just above the foliage mound in late spring, attracting early pollinators. It spreads slowly by short rhizomes into a dense, weed-suppressing groundcover without becoming aggressive, and clumps rarely need dividing except to control size or propagate, typically every three to four years in spring.

common_name: Peachblow Crinum Lily (Heirloom Peachy-Pink Pass-Along Crinum)

planting.note: Plant large bulbs in spring in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface; Peachblow is a long-grown Deep South pass-along crinum, one of the two parents (with Cecil Houdyshel) of the named hybrid Emma Jones.

directions: Plant large bulbs with the neck at or just above the soil surface in well-drained to moist, fertile soil in full sun to partial shade. Peachblow bears clusters of fragrant, trumpet-shaped flowers in a soft peachy-pink that reads warmer and more coral-toned than the plain soft pink of its cross partner Cecil Houdyshel, held on tall scapes above strap-like evergreen foliage. Like other old Southern pass-along crinums, it was grown and shared among gardeners for generations before being widely catalogued, and it persists for decades in old homesteads and cemetery plantings with essentially no care. It tolerates heat, humidity, and a range of soils, blooms in repeated flushes through the warm season, and rarely if ever needs division, since crinum bulbs flower best when left undisturbed and slightly crowded.
sources: Southern Bulb Company — Heirloom Crinum Lily Collection
